corrected_value.title: The cocktail party phenomenon revisited: Attention and memory in the classic selective listening procedure of Cherry (1953).

decision.reason: No prior adjudication or state file exists for this work. The primary text explicitly retests Wood and Cowan (1995), which first introduced the online shadowing-error analysis across word positions around the presentation of one's own name (positions -1, 0, +1, +2, and +3) alongside retrospective name detection (35% vs. 29% here). Shipped row 144 (Moray, 1959, 10.1080/17470215908416289) is a distinct earlier study that measured only retrospective name detection and did not examine shadowing errors by word position; report equivalence does not apply.

corrected_value.authors: Conway AR, Cowan N, & Bunting MF
corrected_value.title: The cocktail party phenomenon revisited: The importance of working memory capacity.

decision.quote:
Replicating the finding of
Conway et al. (2001)
that individual differences in working memory span are related to errors in shadowing after the presentation of one’s own name, low span participants were more likely than high span participants to commit shadowing errors on a relevant to-be-shadowed word location. While this was true regardless of whether participants were classified based on their operation span scores or based on their running span scores, the effect was largest when participants were classified based on both scores combined. Thus it seems the effect is most reliably detected when more than one measure of working memory span is used.
decision.reason: No prior adjudication or state file exists for this work. The study explicitly adopts the operation-span scoring and upper-versus-lower quartile comparison procedure of Conway et al. (2001) to retest whether low-span participants detect their own name more often and commit more shadowing errors at relevant word locations (word, word +1, word +2) than high-span participants. This independent 2001 individual-differences study is absent from shipped row 144 (Moray, 1959) and is distinct from sibling target 1 (Wood & Cowan, 1995).

decision.quote:
Further work on adult aging by
Naveh-Benjamin et al. (2014)
shows that it is not low span per se that drives the individual difference in noticing one’s own name, but span insofar as it relates to control of attention. Specifically, while two thirds of the younger participants noticed their own name in the irrelevant message, older participants rarely did, even though their average span was equivalent to low-span young adults.
decision.reason: No prior adjudication or state file exists for this work. Naveh-Benjamin et al. (2014) investigated adult aging differences in noticing one's own name (older vs. younger adults). The present study tested only a single young-adult sample (N = 80, M age = 25) and did not retest the aging finding of Naveh-Benjamin et al. (2014); its citation in the Introduction as a prior replication and in the Discussion as a literature reference rate for young adults in Experiments 1 and 4 is background context for the basic cocktail-party phenomenon already represented by shipped row 144 (Moray, 1959) and canonical missing targets 1 and 2.

decision.quote:
A priori, it seemed possible to speculate that unexpected words are also noticed during selective listening. Recent evidence from a cross-modal distraction task suggested that the extent of semantic processing in the irrelevant auditory channel tends to be underestimated, because the processing only results in an observable disruption if an unexpected or behaviorally relevant signal is detected (
Röer et al., 2019
; see also
Vachon, Marsh & Labonté, in press
).
decision.reason: No prior adjudication or state file exists for this work. Röer, Bell, Körner, & Buchner (2019) examined semantic mismatch disruption in a cross-modal visual-verbal serial recall task and is cited only as background motivation for the novel extension component of the present study ('The study is the first to investigate whether semantically unexpected words are detected in the irrelevant auditory channel'). Because motivation for an extension to dichotic selective listening is not an empirical retest of the serial-recall study, this candidate is not a missing replication target; the replicated cocktail-party phenomenon is represented by shipped row 144 and missing targets 1 and 2.

No prior adjudication or state file exists for this work. Röer, Buchner, & Bell (in press) is cited only once in the entire paper, jointly with Röer et al. (2019) in the Introduction as background literature on semantic mismatch effects in cross-modal serial recall motivating the paper's novel extension to dichotic selective listening, and is never mentioned in the Method, Results, or Discussion. It is background motivation for an extension rather than an empirically retested original target (and is also co-cited with target 4 while the replicated cocktail-party phenomenon is represented by shipped row 144 and missing targets 1 and 2).

decision.quote:
In order to dig deeper into the results obtained by the CPS, I have tried to replicate this part of the
   research. Of course, without access to the CPS dataset there will be some differences from their
   results, but the methodology I have applied is designed to be transparent and robust in its own
   right.

The blind target ('Bias at the Beeb: A quantitative study of slant in BBC online reporting', unnamed author/year in the blog text) is the exact same Centre for Policy Studies (CPS) report already represented by shipped row 2593 (Latham, 2012, 'Bias at the Beeb?
